Evaluation of different air dosing strategies to enhance H2S removal in 
microaerobic systems treating low-strength wastewaters 
M. R. Sousa1, C. J. S. Oliveira1, J. M. Carneiro1, A. C. Lopes1, E. Rodríguez1, E. A. F. 
Vasconcelos1, G. B. M. Holanda1, P. G. C. Landim1, M. E. R. Silva2, P. I. M. Firmino1, 
A. B. dos Santos1,*. 
 
1 Department of Hydraulic and Environmental Engineering, Federal University of 
Ceará, Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil. 
 
2 Department of Civil Construction, Federal Institute of Science and Technology of 
Ceará, Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil. 
 
* Corresponding Author: Rua do Contorno, S/N Campus do Pici, Bloco 713, Fortaleza, 
Ceará, Brazil, CEP: 60455-900. E-mail: andre23@ufc.br. 
 
Abstract: This study aimed to evaluate different air dosing strategies such as 
microaeration flow rates and air dosing points to enhance H2S removal in microaerobic 
systems treating low-strength wastewaters. Efficiency and stability of the reactors as 
well as biogas quality were assessed, and microbial community changes were evaluated 
using PCR-DGGE technique. The results showed that the air dosing point affected the 
H2S concentration and that air dosing at the headspace promoted the highest H2S 
removal efficiency. The airflow rate also affected the process, since H2S concentration 
in the biogas was higher at 0.1 mL air.min-1 than at 0.3 mL air.min-1. The methane 
concentration in the biogas was also affected by both air dosing point and flow rate, 
since the lowest value was observed at the highest airflow rate of the headspace dosing 
point, due to dilution by the N2 influx applied to the system. The highest productivity 
and operational efficiency were observed at this air dosing point, with this airflow 
(HD0.3), which corroborates with the operational results and the ecological parameters, 
since the microaeration at this stage promoted high bacterial and archaeal species

richness and diversity, optimum functional organization, high COD and H2S removal 
efficiencies. 
 
Keywords: anaerobic treatment; biogas; hydrogen sulfide; microaeration; odor control. 
 
 
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic wastewater treatment is a well-established technology in which 
conversion of complex organic matter into biogas is carried out by different microbial 
species from the Bacteria and Archaea domains [1]. The composition of biogas depends 
on the type of carbon source supplemented and the operational conditions of the reactor 
[2]. Although H2S is usually found in very low concentration in the biogas compared to 
CH4 and CO2, this compound is responsible of some significant problems in wastewater 
treatment plants due to its odorous and corrosive nature, which is highly undesirable in 
energy recovery processes [3]. Furthermore, H2S reacts with metals [4], corroding iron, 
copper, cement etc. [2]. Thus, in order to use biogas for energy recovery purposes, cost-
effective and sustainable methods are needed for sulfide removal. 
Available technologies such as controlling H2S emissions by adding 
sulfidogenesis inhibitors,  adsorption on activated carbon [1], gas washing [4]  and other 
available techniques [5], generally imply high investment and/or operational costs. In 
this context, removing H2S from biogas through microaerobic processes seems to be an 
efficient and sustainable alternative to the high costs and high environmental impact of 
chemical adsorption and precipitation of sulfides [6, 7, 8, 9]. The microaerobic 
biotechnology consists on applying a limited influx of oxygen (O2) into an anaerobic 
bioreactor. This strategy avoids the need for additional units for biological H2S 
oxidation, since sulfide-oxidizing bacteria, which promote H2S oxidation, can be found 
in the inoculated sludge [8]. Furthermore, moderate aeration in anaerobic reactors 
treating wastewaters with high sulfate and/or sulfide concentrations reduces H2S in 
biogas and thus sulfide toxicity to methanogenic archaea. This occurs due to the fact 
that H2S oxidation surpasses other oxidative processes [10]. 
Most of the studies using the microaerobic technology have been performed for 
eliminating H2S during sludge digestion and during the treatment of sulfate-rich 
wastewaters. These studies have already confirm the potential of microaeration for H2S 
removal without promoting negative impacts on anaerobic digestion [9, 10, 11, 12].

However, fewer studies have addressed the potential of this technology for the treatment 
of low-strength wastewaters (low COD and sulfate concentrations). Moreover, further 
investigation is required concerning the process engineering regardless of the type of 
wastewater in order optimize the technology. Key aspects that need to be addressed 
include: the best point for air dosing, the most adequate airflow rate, proper diffusion 
devices, process control, the microbiology of the process, the robustness of the 
technology towards operational failures or fluctuations (shocks loads, interruptions of 
aeration etc.), the improvement of the system capacity for dissolved sulfide removal etc. 
Changes of microbial communities (microbial succession) engineered 
ecosystems (bioreactors) in response to variations in operating conditions constitute a 
main issue in microbial ecology to predict system or ecosystem behavior [13]. Several 
characteristics of the microbial community structure seem to play a key role in 
maintaining functional stability under these variations. For example, richness, evenness, 
dynamics, functional redundancy, microbial composition and microbial interactions 
seem to be of utmost importance for controlling reactor and ecosystem functioning [14, 
15, 16].  
As an example, communities exhibiting intermediate evenness values (some 
species are dominant but most of them are present in decreasing lower amounts) have 
been shown to better deal with changing environmental conditions, since they have a 
pool of less dominant species able to replace the leading ones under operating or 
environmental fluctuations [17]. Species richness effects on ecosystem functioning can 
decrease when functionally redundant species exist in the community [14]. 
This type of studies helps to understand process performance and behavior not 
only in anaerobic but in every biological ecosystem towards fluctuations in 
environmental conditions. Moreover, these studies help to discover general trends that 
can be used to optimize and/or predict the behavior of bioreactors. 
In this context, two microaerobic reactors treating low-strength wastewaters 
were operated in this study aimed at: 1) evaluate the best point for air dosing at different 
zones of the reactor; 2) assess the effects of increasing the airflow rate on H2S and 
dissolved sulfide removal efficiencies; 3) evaluate the operational stability of the 
reactors; 4) assess the quality of the biogas produced. A sulfur balance analysis was 
calculated and bacterial and archaeal communities were studied by means of molecular 
biology techniques for a better understanding of the process and assess the effect of 
oxygen on the anaerobic ecosystem.

2. Material and methods 
2.1. Inoculum and carbon source 
The reactors were inoculated with granular anaerobic sludge according to Sousa, 
Oliveira [9]. 
The feeding consisted of synthetic wastewater with ethanol as the electron donor 
(COD = 1 g.L-1) (99.8% purity, Dinâmica Química, Brazil). According to literature, 
defined substrates, such as lactate, ethanol, methanol and hydrogen, are preferential 
electron donors for sulfate reduction, in which high efficiencies are obtained (~ 80%) 
[18, 19]. The composition of basal medium was according to Firmino, Silva [20]. To 
increase the sulfide concentration in the biogas, sodium sulfate (400 mg∙L-1) was added 
to the basal medium. The influent was stored under refrigeration at a temperature of 
approximately 4 °C. To keep pH around 7.0, the wastewater was buffered with sodium 
bicarbonate (NaHCO3) in the proportion of 1 g NaHCO3 to each 1 g COD ethanol. 
 
2.3. Reactors set up 
The experiment was conducted in two lab-scale continuous-flow anaerobic 
reactors (R1 and R2) with a total volume of 3.5 L each one (working volume of 2.8 L, 
digestion compartment inner diameter of 60 mm, settling compartment inner diameter 
of 85 mm, total height of 820 mm). The reactors were made of acrylic plastic and 
operated at a hydraulic retention time (HRT) of approximately 11 h. An organic loading 
rate (OLR) of about 2.0 kg COD∙m-3∙d-1 was applied. The reactors were fed by a 
peristaltic pump (Watson Marlon, Model 323U/D) at an average flow rate of 6.0 L∙d-1. 
The reactors effluent were recirculated by metering pumps (ProMinent, model Concept 
Plus CNPA 1000 NPB2 00A01) at a flow rate of approximately 1 L∙h-1, which provided 
an upflow velocity of 0.5 m∙h-1. The systems were equipped with electrodes for on-line 
redox potential (ORP) measurements. Biogas production was measured by counting the 
number of pulses generated in a water displacement device (25 mL per pulse). 
 
2.4. Operational strategy 
The R1 system was initially operated under anaerobic conditions (AN) for 155 
days. After that, microaeration was applied above the sludge blanket (ASB) in two 
different airflow rates of 0.1 and 0.3 mL min-1, for 90 and 64 days, respectively. The R2 
system was operated under microaerobic conditions during the whole experiment. Two

microaeration application points (stages) were studied, at the headspace (HD) and 
directly at the sludge blanket (SB) with the same airflow rates (0.1 and 0.3 mL min-1). 
The details about the operational parameters of reactors R1 and R2 during the entire 
experiment are summarized in Table 1. 
 
 
  
2.5. Analytical methods 
Chemical oxygen demand (COD), sulfate and dissolved sulfide were analyzed 
according to APHA [21], whereas biogas characterization was performed according to 
Sousa, Oliveira [9]. Bacterial and archaeal community structure was analyzed by PCR-
DGGE (Ploymerase Chain Reaction Denaturing Gradient Gel Electrophoresis) 
according to [9]. The obtained archaeal and bacterial DGGE gels were analyzed in order 
to calculate the following ecological parameters: evenness/functional organization (Fo), 
ranged weighted richness (Rr) and Shannon diversity index (H) according to [22]. 
 
2.6. Statistical analysis 
The experimental data sets of the different periods were compared to each other 
by the Mann-Whitney Rank Sum test at a 95.0% confidence level [9]. 
 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of different air dosing strategies on COD removal and operational stability 
In the anaerobic phase (AN) of R1, the average COD removal efficiency was 
80% (Table 2). Subsequently, after the microaeration was applied above the sludge 
blanket (ASB), the average values of COD removal were higher than in the anaerobic 
phase: 92% (ASB0.1) and 87% (ASB0.3) (Table 2). However, there was no statistically 
significant difference between the microaerobic periods using different airflow rates 
(ASB0.1, ASB0.3) (p = 0.46). Furthermore, there was no statistically significant 
difference between the stages AN and ASB0.1 (p = 0.33), and between stages AN and 
ASB0.3 (p = 0.32). 
In R2, COD removal efficiencies, when microaeration was applied at the 
headspace, were 89%, using an airflow rate of 0.3 mL min-1 (HD0.3), and 84%, using an 
airflow rate of 0.1 mL min-1 (HD0.1). However, no statistically significant differences 
were observed between these values (p = 0.50). When the microaeration was applied at

the sludge blanket (SB), COD removal efficiencies of 79 (SB0.1) and 84% (SB0.3) were 
recorded, presenting again no statistically significant difference between them (p = 
0.67). 
In this work, the microaeration either applied into the liquid or gaseous phase 
did not show any significant effect on the COD removal capacity of the systems. These 
results are in accordance with Krayzelova, Bartacek [23], who evaluated the 
microaeration at the sludge blanket and found COD removals of 89 and 90%, for the 
anaerobic and microaerobic reactors, respectively. They also did not observe a negative 
effect on the methanogenic activity of the microbiota. 
Regarding operational stability, the reactor was stable during the whole 
experiment, and no pH change (~7.5), VFA accumulation (VFA < 250 mg∙L-1) or 
biomass loss were observed. These results are consistent with those reported in 
literature, since it has been widely observed that the influx of small amounts of O2 into 
anaerobic digesters do not affect negatively the digestion performance [24, 25]. In fact, 
Rodríguez, Lopes [26] and Zhou, Imai [27] found a methanogenic activity decrease due 
to the presence of high sulfide concentrations under anaerobic conditions, and the 
microaeration was a good strategy to recover the activity by oxidizing part of the 
sulfide. Rodríguez, Lopes [26] used COD/SO4
-2 ratios of 2-4 and sulfate concentrations 
of 1440 and 2880 mg∙L-1
. Zhou, Imai [27] used COD/SO4
-2 ratios of 15-20 and sulfate 
concentrations ranging from 300 to 500 mg∙L-1. The COD/SO4
-2 ratio of the current 
experiment was 7, and the sulfate concentration was about 140 mg∙L-1. 
The fact that the reactors in this work were inoculated with granular sludge may 
have contributed to the maintenance of COD and sulfate removal performance, as well 
as methane production, when very low O2 concentrations were applied.  Shen and Guiot 
[28] mentioned that methanogenic microorganisms in granular sludge are more tolerant 
to oxygen than in flocculent sludge. According to those authors, such a behavior is due 
to the presence of a multilayer structure in granular sludge, in which the facultative 
microorganisms are predominant in the outer part of the granule, and the methanogenic 
archaea, more sensible to oxygen, would be protected in the granule core. 
On the other hand, a detrimental effect was not found when the air dosing was 
applied into the liquid phase (ASB and SB) in this work. Likely, the sulfide formed 
from sulfate reduction was not at a concentration, which could cause a toxic effect on 
methanogens. According to the presented results (Table 2), sulfide concentration at all 
stages was lower than 50 mg∙L-1. Lettinga, Pol [29] reported inhibition from 25 to 90%

of the methanogenic activity for a sulfide concentration of 150 mg∙L-1. Karhadkar, 
Audic [30] found a 50% inhibition of the methanogenic activity for sulfide 
concentrations of 100-224 mg∙L-1. 
 
H2S removal 
The operational performance for the different air dosing strategies is shown in 
Table 2. The biogas produced at the anaerobic stage (AN) of R1 contained 0.5% of H2S. 
The airflow applied above the sludge blanket (ASB) at stage ASB0.1 promoted a 
decrease of sulfide concentration to 0.34%. When the airflow rate was increased, during 
stage ASB0.3, sulfide concentration decreased further to 0.17%. 
The microaeration applied directly at the headspace (HD) in R2 also had a 
positive impact on H2S removal, in which the concentrations were 0.07% and 0.03%, 
respectively, for the stages HD0.1 and HD0.3.  
The last microaeration strategy evaluated was directly at the sludge blanket (SB) 
in R2, based on the hypothesis that the flow could strip the dissolved H2S to higher 
zones of the reactor, including the headspace, thus favoring a more effective oxidation 
of sulfide. However, at both stages SB0.3 and SB0.1, the concentration of H2S increased 
up to 4.6 times compared to the level obtained at stage HD0.3, i.e. increasing from 0.03 
to 0.10% (SB0.1) and 0.13% (SB0.3). Therefore, applying air at the sludge blanket zone 
increased a bit the sulfide stripping from the liquid phase but it did not promote an 
efficient H2S removal from the biogas.  
Some investigations report sulfide reductions of 20-30% in the liquid phase and 
high H2S removal from the biogas [23, 27, 31]. It is worth mentioning that most of 
sulfide oxidation was probably taking place at the headspace, even when the air dosing 
was in the liquid phase. 
Krayzelova, Bartacek [23] found that the average concentration of H2S in the 
biogas from a UASB reactor was 8.9 and 2.2 g∙m-3 when operated under anaerobic and 
microaerobic conditions, respectively, representing an improvement of 73% compared 
to the anaerobic phase. They applied microaeration at the feeding line, below the sludge 
blanket, at a flow rate of 0.7 mL∙min-1 air (0.5 mol O2∙mol-1 S-2). These results are in 
accordance with the present investigation, since an improvement of 80% and 74% of 
H2S removal was obtained in phases SB0.1 and SB0.3, respectively, when compared to 
the anaerobic conditions. In the present work, the airflow rates used were 0.1 and 0.3 
mL∙min-1, corresponding to 0.15 and 0.45 mol O2∙mol-1 S-2, respectively.

Moreover, the efficiency of desulfurization was not as high as in other studies 
[24, 32], in which a removal efficiency of 98-99% was observed. However, the dose of 
air or oxygen was much higher in those studies compared to present study. 
When comparing the air dosing strategies, it can be noticed that the 
microaeration at the headspace was the most efficient method for H2S removal in low-
strength wastewaters. These results are similar to those observed by Díaz, Pérez [32] by 
evaluating the microaerobic process in a sludge digester. The latter work assessed 
different air dosing points, and the headspace presented the best performance. Previous 
microbial community analyses have revealed that the sulfide oxidizing bacteria (SOB) 
were growing mainly on the headspace surface wall or on the gas-liquid interface, 
suggesting that the biological sulfide oxidation was occurring at this point [26, 32, 33, 
34]. 
 
SO4
-2 removal 
Under anaerobic conditions (AN), the average removal efficiency reached 83.4% 
(Table 2). Microaeration above the sludge blanket (ASB) during stage ASB0.1 promoted 
an increase in sulfate removal efficiency to 86%. However, at stage ASB0.3, the 
efficiency decreased to 77% (Table 2). A statistically significant difference (p = 0.03) 
was observed between the microaerobic stages ASB0.1 and ASB0.3. The stage ASB0.3 
was also slightly less stable in terms of sulfate reduction, probably due to the higher 
concentration of O2, which might have favored the re-oxidation of sulfide or elemental 
sulfur to sulfate. However, this hypothesis is very unlikely to occur because the molar 
flow rate (mmol O2∙mmol-1 S-2) applied was lower than 0.5. It is reported that, only 
when the molar flow rate is higher than 2.0, sulfide is completely oxidized to sulfate 
[35]. 
Microaeration applied directly at the headspace (HD) provided sulfate reduction 
efficiency of 78% and 81%, at stages HD0.1 and HD0.3, respectively, which were 
statistically similar (p = 0.37) (Table 2). Therefore, apparently the presence of 
microaeration at the headspace and the increase in air dosage did not affect significantly 
the system sulfate removal. 
The levels of sulfate reduction, when the microaeration was applied at the sludge 
blanket point (SB), were 79% and 68%, at stages SB0.1 and SB0.3, respectively (Table 
2). A statistically significant difference (p = 0.01) was observed between the airflow 
rates.

Dissolved sulfide removal 
The mean value of dissolved sulfide concentration at the anaerobic stage (R1) 
was 30 mg∙L-1 (Table 2). Microaeration above the sludge blanket (ASB) at stages 
ASB0.1 and ASB0.3 provided concentrations of 29 and 26 mg∙L-1, respectively, which 
were not statistically different (p = 0.65). Concerning microaeration at the headspace 
(R2), no significant difference (p = 0.61) was observed between the stages HD0.1 and 
HD0.3, reaching concentrations of dissolved sulfide of 25 and 24 mg∙L-1, respectively. 
The sulfide concentration at stages SB0.1 and SB0.3 were identical (24 mg∙L-1) (p = 0.73). 
According to the results, for all air dosing points tested, the increase in the air 
dosage did not have any significant effect on sulfide removal from the liquid phase. 
Moreover, when microaeration was applied above the sludge blanket, sulfide 
concentration increased compared to the anaerobic phase. However, for microaeration at 
either the headspace or the sludge blanket, just a small fraction of the dissolved sulfide 
was removed (16%). 
Dosing air into the liquid phase also caused a decrease in sulfide concentration 
in the liquid phase, usually about 20-30% [23, 27, 31, 32]. Díaz, Pérez [32] reported 
that, when the microaeration was at the headspace, only H2S was possible to be 
removed, and the dissolved sulfide was only removed when microaeration was dosed in 
the liquid phase. 
In the present study, it was possible to remove the dissolved sulfide even when 
the microaeration was at the headspace. As mentioned before, the decrease of dissolved 
sulfide concentration in the liquid phase has the additional positive effect of decreasing 
sulfide toxicity towards methanogens and helping odor control in the treatment plant 
because there is less gas striping in the effluent. 
 
Sulfur mass balance 
A sulfur mass balance was done in order to understand the main flows of sulfur 
conversions. In general, three sulfur flows were considered: sulfur load in terms of 
sulfate (S-SO4
-2) and sulfide (S-S2-) of influent and effluent, as well as hydrogen sulfide 
in the biogas (S-H2S). The elemental sulfur was not considered due to the difficulty of 
measuring it, since it may be adhered to the tubing walls or to the reactor headspace 
inner walls, adsorbed onto the sludge or even as particulate matter in the effluent. Sulfur 
mass balance for the different air dosing strategies is shown in Fig. 1.

It can be noticed that most of the sulfur remained in the liquid phase in the form 
of sulfate (about 20%) and dissolved sulfide (about 65%). The H2S formed, even during 
the anaerobic phase, only represented a very small fraction of the total sulfur (less than 
5%). The gap verified in almost all cases (28-4%) is attributed to the sulfur incorporated 
into the biomass, precipitation of sulfide by some metals present in the micronutrients 
solution, as well as undetected products such as thiosulfate. These findings for gaps in 
mass balance are also reported elsewhere [23, 32, 36]. 
When oxygen is present during the microaerobic process, other factors interfere 
in mass balance, such as formation of elemental sulfur, which can be retained in the 
sludge blanket or even at the headspace of the reactor. In the present experiment, a 
sulfuric mass (similar to elemental sulfur) was found adhered to the inner walls of the 
headspace, a common occurrence, as observed by other authors [23, 32, 36]. 
The elemental sulfur deposition on the headspace wall and tubes may obstruct 
the system, resulting in an overpressure and a biogas leak [26, 32, 33, 34]. However, 
Jeníček, Horejš [7], while monitoring a real scale digester with microaeration at sludge 
recirculation line, did not observe any clogging of the biogas line. According to the 
latter investigation, such a behavior was due to the controlled air dosing in the liquid 
phase, in which most of the oxygen was consumed in the digester. 
During the anaerobic step, 17% of the effluent sulfur was in form of sulfate, and 
62% as dissolved sulfide (Fig. 1). When microaeration was supplemented at the reactor 
headspace (HD0.3), the percentage of dissolved sulfide was reduced to 53%. These 
results are in accordance to the ones reported by Krayzelova, Bartacek [23], who found 
that the sulfide detected in the effluent from microaerobic and anaerobic reactors 
accounted for 41% and 49% of the sulfur dosed, respectively. These authors highlighted 
that the main differences between the anaerobic and microaerobic reactors were the 
amount of hydrogen sulfide in biogas, the deposition of sulfur in the G–L–S separator, 
and solids in the effluent excluding sulfide. According to them, over 33% of sulfur was 
present in the solid phase of the effluent from the microaerobic reactor, while only 6% 
was in the effluent of the anaerobic reactor. Additionally, large part of the elemental 
sulfur oxidized during microaeration also accumulated in the G–S–L separator of the 
microaerobic reactor (10%), even when the microaeration was applied at the bottom of 
the reactor [23]. 
One important point to be observed is that, although the microaeration was very 
effective to remove H2S, being an in situ strategy for biogas treatment, the effect on

dissolved sulfide was not evident, and this fraction showed to be the most important one 
in the effluent mass balance. Therefore, strategies to combine simultaneous H2S and 
dissolved sulfide are very important in order to control odor in treatment plants and 
produce a cleaner biogas. 
 
3.2. Effect of different air dosing strategies on biogas quality 
Average values of concentration (%) and molar flow rate (mmol∙d-1) for the 
gases O2, N2, CH4, CO2, H2S and NH3 are shown in Table 3. 
Methane molar flow rate was higher during the anaerobic stage compared to all 
other stages when microaeration was applied (Table 3). Another aspect is that, when the 
microaeration was higher, methane molar production was lower. Most likely, part of the 
organic matter was oxidized by facultative microorganisms present in the anaerobic 
sludge, which prefer oxygen as electron acceptor, therefore decreasing the organic 
fraction available for anaerobic microorganisms to produce methane. 
Literature also reports a possible use of methane as electron donor when oxygen 
is present, however this is very unlikely to occur in the conditions tested and the source 
of sludge used. According to Ramos, Pérez [37], eventual increases in aerobic activity 
inside the reactor could also explain occasional decreases in methane concentration on 
the biogas. 
As expected, microaeration dilutes the methane in the biogas and increases the 
concentration of oxygen and nitrogen (Table 3). The latter increase is because 
atmospheric air is used as source of oxygen. However, in all cases, the concentration of 
methane is much higher than 40%, which is the limit value for the combustion of 
methane. 
In general, for safety reasons, mixing oxygen or air with biogas is not allowed 
due to the explosion risks of the mix methane/oxygen. However, the inflammable range 
is typically from 5 to 15% methane:air (v:v) [4]. Therefore, the leak of methane in the 
air should be considered a higher risk compared to the mix of a small amount of 
oxygen/air with biogas. 
According to Jeníček, Horejš [7], during the usual microaerobic desulfurization, 
the amount of oxygen in the biogas very unlikely will reach those values. The maximum 
concentration of O2 in the biogas was 0.3% during a full-scale investigation with 
microaerated anaerobic digesters. In the current investigation, the concentration of O2 in

the biogas was by far lower than the threshold limit, which is in agreement with the 
latter investigation. 
CO2 concentration values in biogas are lower than typical values found in biogas 
(Table 3). However, the percentage of CH4 and CO2 in biogas largely depends on the 
feedstock, and on the experimental conditions applied. In this work, ethanol was used as 
the sole carbon and energy source, and its fermentation does not generate directly CO2, 
but it does H2 and acetate, which are methanogenic substrates. In fact, CH4 and CO2 can 
be produced from acetoclastic methanogenesis. However, this CO2 can be used as 
electron acceptor by hydrogenotrophic archaea to produce CH4 from H2. Therefore, it 
might have reduced CO2 concentration in biogas, although further investigation is 
necessary to reinforce this hypothesis. Additionally, microaeration also diluted the CO2 
concentration in the biogas, as reported for methane. 
NH3 molar flow rate was higher during the anaerobic stage compared to all other 
stages when microaeration was applied (Table 3). Probably, a biological reaction was 
taking place, especially when the microaeration was applied to the headspace. However, 
further investigations need to be conducted in order to elucidate if the removal is via 
assimilatory or dissimilatory process. 
 
3.3. Microbial community structure under different air dosing points and airflow rates  
Changes in operational conditions in bioreactors promote changes in microbial 
interactions, leading to the adaptation of the species to the environment imposed. In this 
context, analyzing changes in microbial community structure (Fig. 2) in terms of 
different ecological parameters such as richness, evenness, diversity, etc. during reactor 
operation, have been widely used to understand and trying to predict the behavior of the 
system [17]. Various authors have shown that even a strictly direct correlation between 
the functionality of a biological system and the ecological parameters observed are not 
observed, maintaining certain ecological parameters within certain ranges promotes 
stability of bioreactor performance [15, 38]. 
In this study, bacterial and archaeal communities in the seed sample showed 
richness, functional organization (Fo) and Shannon diversity values within the range 
that, according to previous studies, favor the stability of the reactor due to a rapid 
adaptation of the community [17]. High richness, and diversity as well as a medium 
functional organization were observed (Table 4). In this context, despite the inoculum 
presented optimum characteristics in terms of community structure, a clear impact of

ethanol introduction was observed in the bacterial and archaeal communities of R1 
during stage AN (Table 4). While the bacterial community was slightly affected (a 
reduction in range-weighted richness (Rr) was observed but still remained within the 
range of medium Rr values), the archaeal community suffered a major impact; Fo 
decreased from medium to low values, and Rr decreased from high to low values, with 
the concomitant reduction of H (which includes evenness and richness parameters on its 
calculation). Bacteria present a more versatile metabolism and the community was able 
to rearrange their structure maintaining Fo. On the contrary, in archaea, which possess a 
more 
restricted 
metabolism 
(mainly 
hydrogenotrophic, 
acetoclastic 
and 
methylotrophic), change to a situation in which ethanol was the sole energy and carbon 
source, could have induced a strong variation in the substrates available for methane 
production by archaea from the inoculum sample to the first anaerobic condition (AN) 
in R1, leading to a community with a non-well-defined internal structure in terms of 
species dominance. 
Oxygen introduction in R1 (ASB0.1) led to a slight increase in Rr in bacterial 
communities, likely due to availability of an additional electron acceptor for new 
metabolic reactions (sulfide oxidation, ethanol oxidation). Fo remained at a medium 
value and H was similar, suggesting a low impact of O2 introduction in terms of 
bacterial community structure. At this stage (ASB0.1), archaeal communities were able 
to recover medium Fo values, suggesting the emergence of certain archaeal species as 
dominant, while remaining the vast majority in lower amounts. Rr still remained at low 
values (Table 4). The operation of R1 under microaerobic conditions at an airflow rate 
of 0.3 mL min-1 (ASB0.3) promoted a negative impact on bacterial community, 
decreasing the ecological parameters (Fo from medium to low values, Rr from medium-
high to low values, and H from 2.44 to 1.73). Archaeal communities presented similar 
values than those observed at stage ASB0.1. Despite variations observed in richness and 
evenness of the bacterial and archaeal communities due to the operational conditions, 
R1 remained stable in terms of COD and sulfate removal when oxygen was applied at 
low concentrations. The highly dynamic communities (change in species coming to 
significance) likely ensured good process functionality as previously observed by other 
authors [38]. 
In R2, initially operated under microaerobic conditions at an airflow rate of 
0.3mL min-1 (HD0.3), a slight increase in diversity (H) and Rr (while still within the 
range of medium richness) of bacterial communities was observed likely due to the

availability of O2 as electron acceptor for bacteria (Table 4). Microaeration implies 
more ecological niches to be occupied by bacteria and thus an increase in diversity and 
richness can be observed. Fo remained at its medium values as compared to the 
inoculum sample, suggesting a low impact of feeding change on bacterial populations in 
terms of ecological structure. Similarly, a slight decrease in Rr was observed for archaea 
(while still within the range of high Rr values) and Fo remained at its medium values 
(Table 4). 
The airflow reduction in R2 (HD0.1) promoted a decrease in bacterial and 
archaeal Rr (from 86 (high) to 27 (medium) in bacteria; from 70 (high) to 26 (medium) 
in archaea) and H (from 3.05 to 2.40 in bacteria; form 2.47 to 1.98 in archaea), likely 
due to the low availability of O2 for facultative and aerobic organisms (sulfide 
oxidizers) and to changes in the substrate type for methanogens, while Fo remained at a 
medium value (Table 4). 
When microaeration was supplied at the sludge blanket (SB0.1, SB0.3) major 
changes in Rr, Fo and H were not observed as compared to the previous operation stage 
(HD0.1). A slight increase in diversity and Rr was observed for archaeal and bacterial 
communities but Fo remained at medium values (Table 4). Very similar values of Rr, H 
and Fo were observed between SB0.1 and SB0.3 stages, which corroborates that the 
disturbance applied to the system (increase in airflow rate) was not enough to induce 
shifts in the bacterial community. 
The oxygen at 0.3 mL∙min-1 affected mainly bacterial communities in R1, while 
ecological parameters of archaeal communities remained almost constant. The effects of 
increasing oxygen concentration consisted on a decrease in Fo and Rr parameters 
suggesting the loss of diversity. A plausible explanation could be related to an 
inhibitory effect of O2 on sulfate reducing bacteria, syntrophic bacteria or both, leading 
to the loss of species within these groups. In addition, a decrease of these bacterial 
groups could be related to an increase of aerobic bacteria consuming the substrates 
previously used by these groups. In fact, significant differences in SO4
2- removal were 
observed between ASB0.1 and ASB0.3 suggesting a negative effect of O2 directly on 
SRB, over syntrophic communities providing the SRB growth substrate or caused by 
competition with aerobic microorganisms. Unlike in R1, using an airflow rate of 0.3 
mL∙min-1 did not affect bacterial-related ecological parameters in R2. The fact that R1 
was firstly subjected to an anaerobic phase using ethanol as the sole substrate led to a 
decrease mainly in bacterial and archaeal richness due to reduction in resource variety.

This specialization of anaerobic groups could have influenced the subsequent adaptation 
of these microorganisms when using and airflow rate of 0.3 mL∙min-1 limiting the 
emergence of species able to tolerate such oxygen concentrations. On the contrary, R2 
was not subjected to this specialization since it was directly operated under 
microaerobic conditions at an airflow rate of 0.3 mL∙min-1. In fact, authors have 
reported the importance of the inoculum characteristics, mainly diversity, to stablish a 
good microbial community in terms of functionality [38]. 
Despite variations observed in ecological parameters measured in this study, a 
weak correlation was observed between these variations and the functional performance 
of the systems in terms of COD and sulfate removal, which remained almost stable 
along the whole reactor operation in R1 and R2. However, the higher levels of richness 
and diversity for archaea and bacteria were observed for the sample corresponding to 
HD0.3, when the best sulfide removal capacity was recorded (Table 2), suggesting a 
higher availability of oxygen to sulfide oxidizers under this conditions. 
 
4. Conclusions 
The microaeration at the headspace represents a feasible and efficient strategy 
for sulfate and H2S removal in low-strength wastewaters. The best airflow was 0.3 
mL∙min-1 (HD0.3), resulting in the lowest H2S (< 0.1%) concentration, whereas CH4 
concentration remained above 60%. 
The highest productivity and operational efficiency was observed at this air 
dosing point, with this airflow (HD0.3), which corroborates with the operational results 
and the ecological parameters, since the microaeration at this stage promoted high 
bacterial and archaeal species richness and diversity, optimum functional organization, 
high COD and H2S removal efficiency.
